absent: Numeric values and bit layouts of hypercall codes, status codes, flush flags, generic set formats, vector bounds, repeat offset, connection mask, flush-all marker, FIFO size, bank limits and maximum vCPU count.
Partition-wide versus per-vCPU register identifier sets and their read and write semantics beyond dispatch and locking.
Initialization, sizing, lifetime and full locking discipline for VM-wide and per-vCPU Hyper-V state, flush queues, masks and scratch banks.
Behavior of nested address translation, flush request handling, APIC injection, event connection management, guest page access, tracing and statistics beyond what fragments show.
Complete fast versus slow hypercall convention, full dispatch and validation, and userspace exit protocol.
Canonical address calculation and capability detection beyond width selection, and protected-state handling beyond hypercall width.

findings.text: Common Hyper-V model register accessors gate guest access on per-vCPU enablement and ensure per-vCPU Hyper-V state exists, then dispatch partition-wide identifiers to a partition-wide handler and other identifiers to a per-vCPU handler, reporting unhandled status when disabled or initialization fails.

Per-vCPU TLB flush drain requires two-dimensional paging and a valid per-mode flush queue, consumes queued address entries while skipping addresses deemed noncanonical for invalidation, accounts each consumed address group, and signals need for a full flush when a flush-all marker is encountered.

CPUID enforcement control lazily creates per-vCPU Hyper-V state when enforcement is requested, succeeds without state when enforcement is cleared and no state exists, and otherwise records the enforcement flag on existing state.

Masked vCPU request helper walks set positions in a caller bitmap, issues the same request number to each existing target while accumulating host CPUs needing a kick, performs a single kick operation with wait semantics derived from the request number, and reports whether a kick was issued.

Guest memory read helper transfers a byte range starting at a guest physical address by splitting at host page boundaries and issuing one per-page read per segment, advancing through successive guest frames and stopping with an error on the first failing segment.

Hypercall descriptor carries guest-provided addresses and operation selectors including variable and repeat counts and repeat index plus fast and repeat flags, a fixed set of vector registers for fast inputs, and a shared progress field reused as a guest-memory byte offset for slow calls or a consumed half-register count for fast calls.
Partition-wide Hyper-V register accesses serialize on a VM-wide mutex held only around the partition-wide handler, while per-vCPU register accesses use no such guard in these wrappers.

TLB flush queue insertion serializes writers with a per-queue spin lock, and queue selection depends on whether the requesting vCPU runs nested, with a safe lookup that can yield no queue and then insertion becomes a no-op.
Hyper-V connection to event notification lookup runs under read-side RCU protection, relying on a separate sleepable RCU domain to keep the looked-up notification object alive during signaling.

Sparse virtual processor sets encode membership as a valid-bank mask plus densely packed present banks in ascending order with a fixed processor count per bank, and single-bank legacy forms are represented as only bank zero valid.

Extended flush and extended send operations require the supplied variable bank count to equal the population count of the valid-bank mask, reject larger counts and mismatches as invalid input, and treat an explicitly empty sparse set as immediate success without further work.

Fast hypercall variable data is drawn from halves of vector registers after skipping halves already consumed by fixed parameters, with the original count still validated against register capacity even when surplus banks are ignored via a cap, while slow calls read from guest memory at the current offset.

Canonicality for invalidation, model register and descriptor-table loads uses host maximum virtual width, while other emulation uses the vCPU width; both widths select wide mode when large addressing is available or enabled and narrow mode otherwise.

Queued TLB flush entries either hold a page-aligned address with a low-bit count of additional pages or a dedicated flush-all marker, and producers always leave room for one marker so exhaustion can be represented.
Legacy flush requests with all-processors flag set or with a zero processor mask target every processor, preserving compatibility with guests that emit an empty mask while expecting a flush.

Synthetic interrupt injection requires an in-kernel local APIC, delivers fixed-mode interrupts only, validates the requested vector against Hyper-V low and high bounds, and distinguishes all-processors form from sparse-bank form without fetching banks for the former.

Slow signal-event calls validate that the guest address for the connection identifier is naturally aligned and contained within one page before reading it, reject nonzero flag subfields as an invalid port and other reserved bits as invalid input, and map a missing connection to invalid port.

Flush distribution has three modes: host-wide broadcast enqueues to every vCPU host queue and requests all; host selective converts the sparse set to a host mask and requests only members; nested mode keeps only vCPUs sharing the requestor nested domain and passing sparse membership, enqueues to their nested queues and requests that mask, always reporting repeat completion equal to repeat count on success.

Hypercall completion for successful nested flush operations rereads a lock word from a nested shared page and converts read failure into invalid input, then publishes the result to guest register state, accounts the hypercall, advances past the emulated instruction, and conditionally requests a synthetic exit when the lock word is nonzero.
Userspace-completed hypercalls resume through a helper that forwards the result supplied in the shared run structure into the normal completion path.

Guest physical translation is identity when nesting is inactive or when already walking nested addresses, and otherwise delegates to the registered nested translation operation with supplied access and exception context.
Hypercall result publication selects full-width return register handling for sixty-four-bit guests including protected-state guests, and split high and low return registers otherwise.

When queued entries do not fit while preserving one free slot, or when no entry list is supplied for address-space flushes or oversized repeat counts, producers record only a flush-all marker and consumers fall back to a full flush, so queue pressure upgrades selective flushes to full flushes.

Nested flush target filtering can race with nested vCPUs entering, exiting or migrating between host vCPUs; correctness relies on full flushes on migration or context switch except when the target stays on the same host vCPU from request through handling.

Sparse-to-mask conversion optimizes for identity between virtual-processor index and vCPU position using a mismatch hint, falling back to per-vCPU index tests when mismatches exist, so staleness only affects which path is taken while correctness depends on the current index mapping.

Flush and send hypercalls are distinguished by dedicated operation codes for base and extended address-list and address-space forms and for base and extended synthetic interrupts, with extended forms using a generic set format that selects between all-processors and sparse bank encodings.

Successful flush returns combine a success status with repeat completion equal to the requested repeat count placed at a defined hypercall repeat offset, and connection identifiers are constrained by a defined mask with a reserved flag subfield.
